query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Inducing a controlled level of chemical short‐range order (SRO) in the originally random HfNbTaTiZr BCC solid-solution restricts edge dislocation glide at elevated temperatures, which in turn moderates thermal expansion and yields a near-plateau stress–strain response and a more isotropic elastic behavior relative to the baseline random alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy in the as-cast, single-phase BCC solid-solution state with a statistically random distribution of constituent elements.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted heat treatment protocol (e.g., annealing at a defined elevated temperature for a controlled duration) designed to promote the formation of measurable chemical short-range order without inducing secondary phases.
generation.conditions: Mechanical and thermal tests performed in the temperature range from approximately 600 K to 1073 K under controlled loading (e.g., constant strain rate tensile or nanoindentation tests) and dilatometry for thermal expansion measurements; comparison performed between the baseline (random alloy) and the SRO-enhanced alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemical short-range order induced within the BCC lattice, further enhancing local lattice distortions.
generation.mechanism: The formation of SRO increases local atomic ordering, which enhances lattice distortion and creates pinning sites that hinder edge dislocation motion. This inhibited dislocation mobility is predicted to lead to a limited softening (i.e. a plateau in yield strength), a reduced and more uniform thermal expansion, and an elastic response that remains nearly isotropic at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline random alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under elevated temperature mechanical and thermal testing, the SRO-enhanced HfNbTaTiZr sample will show (a) a higher or more stable yield strength (i.e. a less pronounced decrease in the stress–strain curve), (b) a reduced thermal expansion coefficient, and (c) less variation between directional elastic moduli compared to the baseline random alloy.
generation.baseline: HfNbTaTiZr alloy in the as-cast, randomly distributed solid solution state.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for tests performed in the elevated temperature regime (roughly 600 K to 1073 K) and under quasi-static or nanoindentation loading conditions where dislocation-mediated plasticity is dominant; it may not extend to temperatures or strain rates where phase transformation or kinetic roughening processes dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative differences in yield strength retention, thermal expansion reduction, and elastic isotropy are not predicted due to insufficient prior data; the predicted trends are qualitative. The optimal heat treatment parameters to reproducibly induce SRO without undesirable phase precipitation are also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set as baseline (as-cast, random solid solution) and one set subjected to the controlled heat treatment aimed at inducing SRO. Conduct identical high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or nanoindentation tests from 600 K to 1073 K) and dilatometry measurements on both sets. Compare the yield strengths, thermal expansion coefficients, and elastic moduli (including anisotropy measures derived from orientation-resolved measurements).
measurements: Stress–strain curves to extract yield strength and flow behavior at specified temperatures
Dilatometry to measure linear thermal expansion coefficients
In situ or ex situ elastic modulus measurements (e.g., resonant ultrasound spectroscopy or in situ neutron diffraction) to assess elastic isotropy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SRO-enhanced samples do not exhibit a statistically significant shift toward higher yield strength retention, reduced thermal expansion, and decreased elastic anisotropy compared to the baseline random alloy under the identical test conditions, then the hypothesis that SRO mediates the observed high-temperature responses is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The plastic response of the Senkov HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy is explored by means of simulated nanoindentation tests. Both a random alloy and an alloy with chemical short-range order are investigated and compared to the well understood case of an elementary Ta crystal. Strong differences in the dislocation plasticity between the alloys and the elementary Ta crystal are found. The high-entropy alloys show only little relaxation of the indentation dislocation network after indenter retraction and only negligible dislocation emission into the sample interior. Short-range order—besides making the alloy both stiffer and harder—further increases the size of the plastic zone and the dislocation density there. These features are explained by the slow dislocation migration in these alloys. Also, the short-range-ordered alloy features no twinning plasticity in contrast to the random alloy, while elemental Ta exhibits twinning under high stress but detwins considerably under stress relief. The results are in good qualitative agreement with our current knowledge of plasticity in high-entropy alloys.

There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.
